justification: Both real top-ranking pages for 'virtual memory explained' are plain static HTML with no dark theme, no responsive diagram handling and no runnable code: Wikipedia's article leans on a single static PNG (a decades-old-style page-table box diagram) with dense unbroken prose and no mobile-specific layout; GeeksforGeeks intersperses ad units between sections, uses a handful of low-resolution raster diagrams that do not adapt to theme or viewport, and never shows real measured numbers, only textbook figures. This article clearly exceeds both on the design/UX axis: two hand-written SVG diagrams (Figure 1 address translation, Figure 2 TLB hit-vs-walk) that stay legible, correctly themed and unclipped at both 390px and desktop widths in every screenshot checked (all 8 desktop-light parts, all 12 mobile-dark parts read in full, plus spot checks of desktop-dark and mobile-light at fold, both figures and the two VirtualAlloc/MemoryMappedFile output panels); the writer sidestepped the biggest mobile risk in the brief by wildcarding every dynamic byte/MB/GB figure in the 'text output' panels with '[...]' rather than printing literal run-to-run numbers, so the panels stay column-aligned and well inside the ~40-char mobile window in both themes, with the real measured numbers (e.g. '2,233,454 MB virtual, 6 MB private, 19 MB working set') living in prose where they wrap normally instead of forcing horizontal scroll; the :::pitfall callout (double-counted working-set pages) renders with a clearly distinct red/pink border and icon in both light and dark; all three exercises stay correctly collapsed (<details>/'Show solution') in every screenshot; heading hierarchy is clean H2-only across the 7-question structure with no level skips; and the prerequisites crosslink to the still-draft processes-and-threads article is handled exactly per WRITER_GUIDE.md §6 — the inline prose mention ('the article on processes and threads', 'the processes-and-threads article') is plain text with no markdown link, and the front-matter 'prerequisites' field is resolved generically by ArticleLayout.astro against the article set it was built with, so it renders as a real 'Before you read' link inside this --drafts build (both articles are drafts) and will simply not render at all in a production build until processes-and-threads is published — there is no broken-link risk either way, confirmed by report.json's broken: []. Real numbers: Lighthouse 99/100/100/100 (only 1 point off a perfect performance score), zero console errors, zero broken links (27 internal links, 13 external checked), mobileOverflowPx 0. Held back from a full 10 by two minor, non-blocking issues: the 1-point performance shortfall traces to shared page-shell sub-audits (bf-cache, max-potential-FID) rather than this article's markup, and Lighthouse ran on a machine with other worktrees potentially building concurrently, so the number should be treated as a lower bound, not a precise one.

issues.problem: Lighthouse performance is 99/100 (well clear of the round's ≥90 gate) but lighthouse.json's failing sub-audits are all shared-shell issues: max-potential-fid scores 0.59 (220ms), 'Page prevented back/forward cache restoration' scores 0 (2 failure reasons), unused-css-rules scores 0.5 (13 KiB), and a document-latency-insight/network-dependency-tree-insight pair flag ~94 KiB of document-request latency. None of these come from the article body (diagrams, code blocks, callouts).
